1	# Task 10: Procedural lighthouse
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. Model a coastal lighthouse entirely from code (no external model, texture or image files). It must read clearly as a lighthouse: a tapered tower with alternating painted bands (at least 3 bands in two contrasting colours), a gallery balcony with a railing near the top, a glass lantern room with a visible lamp, a conical or domed roof with a finial, a door and at least 4 small windows spiralling or stacked up the tower, and a rocky base made of several irregular rocks sitting on a patch of sea or ground. Add a small keeper's cottage next to the base. The camera must frame the whole lighthouse with some sky/horizon visible and slowly orbit it. Use lighting that gives clear form (a key light with shadows plus fill). When the first frame has rendered, set window.__TASK_STATE__ = { ready: true, partCount: <number of distinct visible mesh parts you created>, bandCount: <number of tower bands> }.

content.thinking: I'm figuring out the right scale and radius ratios to shape a frustum using the cylinder primitive, computing top radius relative to bottom diameter, and checking how the cone primitive's default sizing works for comparison.

I'm reconsidering how to approximate a cone shape, thinking a cylinder primitive with radiusTop set to 0 and radiusBottom at 0.5 should give a pointed roof without needing a separate cone primitive.

For rocks I'll use squashed low-poly spheres with irregular rotations and non-uniform scaling to fake faceted stone shapes, and I'm planning to track every primitive with a counter helper so the total mesh count stays around 100-150. For the overall layout I'm starting with the sea as a large flat plane, then building a raised ground island as a short wide cylinder to host the cottage.

Now I'm working out the lighthouse tower structure: a stone plinth base, a tapering series of alternating red and white cylindrical bands rising to about 13 units, with small windows placed in a spiral pattern up the height, plus a ring of rocks and a rock mound at the base.

Confirming the Y-axis rotation maps the box's local z-axis outward correctly, then I'm adding window frame boxes behind each window and planning the door placement at the base of the cottage.

Now I'm working out the gallery platform at the tower's top: a cylinder deck with a tapered corbel bracket beneath it, plus a ring of thin railing posts and a torus top rail circling the edge.

I'll place individual boxes for each rail segment rather than instancing, computing each segment's midpoint angle to position and rotate it so it sits tangent to the circle, matching the rotation convention to the local box axes.

For the lantern room, I'm planning a glass cylinder shell with vertical mullions, an emissive sphere lamp with an internal point light, and base/top rings — I'll need to check what transparency options the material spec supports since true glass transparency might need a pbr opacity setting instead of a dedicated glass material.

I'm figuring out the shadow configuration, deciding on a larger extent value to make sure the shadow coverage doesn't clip the cottage at the edges even if I'm uncertain whether extent means half-size or full-size.

Now I'm laying out the island's geography: positioning the cottage, sizing a central grass cylinder with slightly irregular squashed-sphere edges, placing the tower plinth at the origin, and scattering grey rock formations around the plinth and coastline to cover the gap between the island edge and surrounding sea.

For the cottage itself, I'm working out its box-shaped body dimensions and figuring out a gabled roof made of two tilted slabs meeting at a ridge, calculating the pitch angle, slab length, and ridge height so the roof geometry fits cleanly over the body.

Leaving the gable ends open would expose the hollow interior, so I need to fill them with a triangular prism — a cylinder with 3 radial segments, rotated so its triangular cross-section stands at the end of the roof, matching the base width and slope height.

Actually, a simpler fix is to switch to a hip roof: a 4-sided pyramid (cone with radialSegments 4, rotated 45° in yaw) sized to match the box footprint, which naturally closes off all sides without needing separate gable fillers.
